item.title: Hollywood: Is the Sequel Machine Hitting Its Limit?
item.comments: In 2026, several big-budget sequels flopped in theaters while original films became hits: is betting on franchises still as safe as it used to be?
item.category: 🟢 Original films keep gaining ground for good","🔵 Studios keep betting on sequels despite the flops","🔴 Big-budget sequel flops pile up, studios start cutting
item.description:
The question at hand: In 2026, several big-budget sequels flopped in theaters while original films became hits: is betting on franchises still as safe as it used to be?

The facts: In 2026, the share of sequels and remakes in the US top 10 box office dropped to 50%, from 90% in 2024, while at least three franchises with budgets over $150 million (Star Wars, Masters of the Universe, Supergirl) flop in theaters.

The 3 scenarios:
🟢 Original films keep gaining ground for good
🔵 Studios keep betting on sequels despite the flops
🔴 Big-budget sequel flops pile up, studios start cutting

Which one is most likely? 👉 Read the 3 numbered forecasts on the site — it's free (~6 min read).

Want to vote before seeing the real probabilities? Join our Telegram channel: t.me/scenario_fr

Question or feedback? Just reply to this email, we read every one.
item.source:
After several big-budget sequels flopped in theaters in 2026, does the franchise model that has powered Hollywood for twenty years remain as profitable as before?
In 2026, the share of sequels and remakes in the US top 10 box office dropped to 50%, from 90% in 2024, while at least three franchises with budgets over $150 million (Star Wars, Masters of the Universe, Supergirl) flop in theaters.
The most likely outcome (48%): studios keep up their pace of sequels despite the flops, carried by expected big hits like Avengers: Doomsday, without changing strategy or facing a real financial crisis.
Signal to watch: how Avengers: Doomsday performs at the box office when it opens on December 18, 2026, and whether Disney or Universal announce new budget cuts when they report quarterly results in early 2027.
Our assessment of the impact for France: fairly positive. The favorable (27%) and stable (48%) scenarios, a combined 75% probability, both benefit France's historically strong theatrical market share; only the degraded scenario (25%), by reducing the number of American releases and therefore overall attendance, would weigh on French exhibition as a whole.

item.source:
US tech giants are pledging hundreds of billions of dollars to artificial intelligence: is this revolution catching up with the spending, or are markets on the brink of a crash?
The four largest US tech groups will spend $725 billion in 2026 to build AI infrastructure, up 77% year-on-year, while the IMF and the Bank of England already compare stock valuations to those of the dot-com bubble of 2000.
Most likely (45%): the bubble keeps growing without bursting right away, buoyed by very real profits at the tech giants, despite increasingly visible signs of fragility in the riskiest financing structures.
Signal to watch: the quarterly results of US tech giants, especially Q4 2026 (published late January-February 2027), when investors will judge whether AI-related revenue growth finally justifies these sums.
Our assessment of the impact for France: fairly negative. The stable scenario, the most likely (45%), leaves French savings exposed to a growing bubble without capturing its benefits; the degraded scenario (35%) would expose them directly to a crash. Together, these two scenarios carry an 80% probability, against just 20% for an orderly, favorable normalization.

item.title: Does France Have Three Faces?
item.comments: Metropolises concentrate the wealth, banlieues stay stuck despite the proximity, rural areas decline: is France still moving forward as one country?
item.category: 🟢 A real catch-up plan narrows both fractures","🔵 The gap neither closes nor widens","🔴 The fractures deepen further
item.description:
The question: Metropolises concentrate the wealth, banlieues stay stuck despite the proximity, rural areas decline: is France still moving forward as one country?

The facts: In the March 2026 municipal elections, the National Rally and its allies went from 22 to 74 town halls in rural areas, while the banlieues, for their part, stay stuck with unemployment twice the national average (16.6%) and record abstention — two distinct fractures that France's big metropolises barely feel.

The 3 scenarios:
🟢 A real catch-up plan narrows both fractures
🔵 The gap neither closes nor widens
🔴 The fractures deepen further

Which one is most likely? 👉 Read the 3 numbered forecasts on the site — it's free (~7 min read).

Want to vote before you know the real probabilities? Join the Telegram channel: t.me/scenario_fr

item.source:
The metropolises, the banlieues, and rural France vote, live, and work in increasingly different ways: can the country still move forward as one whole?
In the March 2026 municipal elections, the National Rally and its allies went from 22 to 74 town halls in rural areas, while the banlieues, for their part, stay stuck with unemployment twice the national average (16.6%) and record abstention — two distinct fractures that France's big metropolises barely feel.
Most likely (45%): neither catch-up nor further worsening on either front — current measures (France Ruralités, NPNRU, anti-discrimination testing) continue at the same pace without closing the gaps, while the RN and La France Insoumise each consolidate their positions.
Signal to watch: the content of the 2027 budget for local governments, the France Ruralités plan, and the NPNRU, to be debated this fall, and how RN polling and banlieue abstention evolve as spring 2027 approaches.
Our assessment of the impact for France: fairly negative. The stable scenario, the most likely (45%), keeps two already-existing fractures in place without closing them; the degraded scenario (35%) would make them worse still. Together, these two scenarios carry an 80% probability, against just 20% for a genuine catch-up on both fronts.

item.source:
Is OpenAI's bid for a $1 trillion IPO going to pay off?
Valued at $852 billion since March 2026 — a figure unchanged during the $7 billion employee stock buyback held in August —, OpenAI is aiming for the symbolic $1 trillion threshold for its stock market listing.
Most likely (55%): the timeline slips to 2027 without changing the price, as confirmed in late August by CFO Sarah Friar, giving profitability — expected for 2029-2030 — more time to reassure the markets.
Signal to watch: OpenAI's next announcement on timeline or valuation, and the trajectory of its annualized revenue (already up 35% this quarter), which needs to convince Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley that the $1 trillion threshold is within reach.
Our assessment of the impact for France: slightly positive. The stable scenario, the most likely at 55%, buys a little breathing room for European players like Mistral AI before an American giant consolidates its position — but the two extreme scenarios, a resounding success (20%) or a broad valuation shock (25%), would each remain unfavorable for France.

item.source:
Can the partnership the EU just announced for Greenland actually shield the territory from American pressure?
The European Union announced €200 million in investment for Greenland on September 6-7, 2026, and is proposing to double its long-term aid to €530 million for 2028-2034, while Donald Trump has repeated since January 2025 that he wants to take over the territory.
Most likely (50%): the status quo continues — the EU deepens ties mostly through funding, Denmark keeps sovereignty, and Trump keeps up rhetorical pressure without any new concrete escalation.
Signal to watch: whether the €530 million gets confirmed in the EU's 2028-2034 budget, and any new statement or tariff threat from Trump in the weeks following this visit.
Our assessment of the impact for France: fairly negative. The stable (50%) and degraded (30%) scenarios add up to 80% of the odds and leave France — which deployed troops to Greenland in early 2026 — facing an American ally always ready to pressure a European territory, with no lasting solution found. Only the favorable scenario, at 20%, would truly defuse the tension.

item.title: Women's Sport: The Law Now Requires Sharing the Money
item.comments: France's law of August 3, 2026 requires financial solidarity between men's and women's professional sport, without setting any amount: will the funding gap actually narrow?
item.category: 🟢 Federations set an amount and women's budgets rise","🔵 The obligation stays without an amount and budgets barely move","🔴 Men's sport money shrinks and more women's teams shut down
item.description:
The question: France's law of August 3, 2026 requires financial solidarity between men's and women's professional sport, without setting any amount: will the funding gap actually narrow?

The facts: In handball, the only French team sport where both top divisions publish their accounts for the same season, a women's club has €2.74 million on average in 2026-2027, against €6.16 million for a men's Starligue club; a female player there earns €3,273 gross per month, a male player €6,279.

The 3 scenarios:
🟢 Federations set an amount and women's budgets rise
🔵 The obligation stays without an amount and budgets barely move
🔴 Men's sport money shrinks and more women's teams shut down

Which one is most likely? 👉 Read the 3 numbered forecasts on the site — it's free (~7 min read).

Want to vote before you know the real probabilities? Join the Telegram channel: t.me/scenario_fr

A question, a comment? Just reply to this email, we read it.
item.source:
Can a law narrow the money gap between men's and women's sport when it writes down no amount at all?
In handball, the only French team sport where both top divisions publish their accounts for the same season, a women's club has €2.74 million on average in 2026-2027, against €6.16 million for a men's Starligue club; a female player there earns €3,273 gross per month, a male player €6,279.
Most likely (50%): solidarity stays an obligation to report with no precise sum attached, women's budgets gain a few points a year as they did before the law, and the gap stays where it is.
Signal to watch: the publication of the implementing decrees, including the one defining the annual report, then the federations' first report to the sports minister and the Standing Conference on Women's Sport, expected at the end of the 2026-2027 season.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. The stable and degraded scenarios together add up to an 80% chance, and both leave French sportswomen far from the resources of their male counterparts — the stable one by freezing the gap, the degraded one by widening it. Only the favorable scenario, at 20%, would genuinely narrow it.

The facts: In the first half of 2026, Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips sold $6.8 billion at auction, up 70% year-on-year — but ultra-contemporary art strings together a fourth straight year of decline, at $229.9 million in 2025, against a 2021 peak of $742.2 million.

🟢 The market rebalances toward emerging artists

🔴 The top of the market turns too, the crisis becomes general

item.source:
Is the art market experiencing an across-the-board rebound, or a lasting fracture between its top and everything else?
In the first half of 2026, Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips sold $6.8 billion at auction, up 70% year-on-year — but ultra-contemporary art strings together a fourth straight year of decline, at $229.9 million in 2025, against a 2021 peak of $742.2 million.
The most likely scenario (55%): the top of the market keeps setting records while emerging art and mid-tier galleries keep declining, with no crash and no rebalancing in sight.
Signal to watch: the flagship sales of Frieze London and the New York houses in October-November 2026, and the final full-year tally of ultra-contemporary art at the end of 2026.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. With an 85% chance that the stable and degraded scenarios (55% and 30%) keep weakening the mid-range market where most of Paris's art activity is concentrated, against only a 15% chance that the favorable scenario's rebalancing eases it.

item.source:
After five delays since 2019, the United States and China are relaunching their race to put humans on the Moon — this time for good.
On March 24, 2026, NASA unveiled a $20 billion, seven-year plan to build a permanent lunar base, but its own crewed landing timeline — now targeted for 2028 with Artemis IV — has already slipped five times since 2019.
The most likely scenario (50%): technical tests keep progressing on both sides, but the date of the first landing slips once again, toward 2029 or 2030, without either program actually stopping.
Signal to watch: the uncrewed Mengzhou-1 test flight, due in late 2026, and Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket returning to flight after its May 28 explosion.
Our assessment of the impact on France: slightly positive. With a 70% chance that the favorable and stable scenarios (20% and 50%) keep the flow of space contracts already secured by Thales Alenia Space in Cannes, against a 30% risk that a budget cut or the abandonment of a program puts them in question.

item.title: Banned Pesticides: Can Anses Really Say No?

item.description:

The facts: The emergency farming law, validated by the Constitutional Council on August 14, 2026 and enacted on August 19, allows Anses to grant a temporary derogation for acetamiprid and flupyradifurone, two pesticides banned in France since 2018, for 4 struggling farming sectors (hazelnut, apple, cherry, sugar beet).

item.source:
Can Anses really refuse to re-authorize two banned pesticides, as promised by the law that hands it this decision?
The emergency farming law, validated by the Constitutional Council on August 14, 2026 and enacted on August 19, allows Anses to grant a temporary derogation for acetamiprid and flupyradifurone, two pesticides banned in France since 2018, for 4 struggling farming sectors (hazelnut, apple, cherry, sugar beet).
The most likely scenario (45%): Anses grants the derogation exactly within the scope set by the law, for a maximum of three years, without expanding it further.
Signal to watch: Anses's decision, expected by late October 2026, two months after being referred the case by the Agriculture Minister.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. The stable scenario (45%) and the degraded scenario (30%) both bring pesticides banned on health and environmental grounds back into French fields, at least partly — against just a 25% chance that Anses holds the line and refuses the derogation.

Can French professional football find a stable economic model after the collapse of its TV rights?
Since Mediapro's collapse in 2020 and DAZN's departure in 2025, Ligue 1's domestic TV rights have been cut by more than a factor of five: clubs shared just €80.5 million net for the 2025-2026 season, against roughly €500 million a season before the crisis.
The most likely scenario (45%): Ligue 1+, the league's own channel, keeps growing slowly toward 1.2 to 1.3 million subscribers without ever reaching profitability, while clubs keep managing their books under very tight constraints, with no fresh wave of bankruptcies.
Signal to watch: Ligue 1+'s subscriber count when the international break resumes in November 2026, and the DNCG's rulings on clubs' projected accounts.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. The two most likely scenarios combined (80%, stable and degraded) keep or worsen a league that's already well below its pre-crisis funding level — only the favorable scenario (20%) would reverse that trajectory.

Can movie theaters keep holding their ground against streaming?
The global theatrical box office is targeting $34.7 billion in 2026, its best year since 2019, driven by an unprecedented agreement among studios to keep every film in exclusive theatrical release for 45 days before streaming.
The most likely scenario (45%): the 45-day deal holds exactly as is, with no further progress, and the global box office plateaus between $34 and $36 billion, without catching up to the 2019 level.
Signal to watch: Universal's announced move to seven weekends of exclusivity (about 49 days) planned for 2027, and the year-end financial results of the major theater chains (AMC, Cineworld/Regal).
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly positive. The two most likely scenarios combined (75%, favorable and stable) extend the best year for French theaters since 2019 — only the degraded scenario (25%), which would break the window deal, would threaten that momentum.
